extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators and education researchers (teachers, curriculum designers, teacher-researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for bringing aesthetic considerations (beauty, elegance, simplicity, economy, fit, etc.) into school mathematics and for assessing students' aesthetic mathematical capacities. Emphasises pedagogical contexts, negotiation, and types of aesthetic criteria beyond expert conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic terms as evaluative tools ('elegant', 'beautiful')
rubrics_metrics.description: The evaluative role of the aesthetic pervades the world of the professional mathematician where terms such as ‘elegant’ are regularly used to judge ‘good’ theorems, solutions and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and teach the use of aesthetic vocabulary (elegant, beautiful, elegant solution) as legitimate evaluative language; show examples of how mathematicians use such terms to distinguish better from worse mathematical products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid expert-conformity as sole goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not take students' failure to agree with mathematicians' judgements as evidence they lack aesthetic sense; educators should not aim solely to train students to adopt experts' aesthetic judgements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design learning contexts that allow students to develop their own aesthetic preferences appropriate to their goals and needs instead of measuring students by agreement with 'expert' assessments (critique of Dreyfus & Eisenberg's objectivist view).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit aesthetic criteria (economy, cleverness, brevity, simplicity, structure, clarity, surprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic qualities often invoked include economy, cleverness, brevity, simplicity, structure, clarity or surprise in mathematical products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these named criteria when prompting students to reflect on and compare solutions; provide exemplars showing how each criterion can be seen in a proof, construction or method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value-oriented context of negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be invited into a value-oriented context of negotiation rather than a right/wrong context; this allows familiarisation and social negotiation of the worth of particular ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting the 'expert' solution as the right one immediately; instead let students compare, discuss, and 'live through' different solution paths before asking them to make value judgements (contrasts with Dreyfus & Eisenberg study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process- and history-sensitive aesthetics (appreciation of struggle and genealogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students may prefer 'messy, difficult-to-remember formulations' because they encapsulate personal history with a problem and the struggle to solve it; such processual elements can be aesthetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that aesthetic value can come from the history or process of solving (not only the neat end product); invite students to reflect on and share their solution paths, sketches, and guesses as part of aesthetic evaluation (Brown's findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal ownership of solutions as an aesthetic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Students often prefer methods they discovered themselves; ownership and the relation of the solution to the student's perspective are sources of aesthetic preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage student-generated solutions and treat 'it is mine' as a legitimate reason for aesthetic preference; teachers can capitalise on ownership to further engagement and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of fit between problem and solution
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetic 'sense of fit'—how well a method answers the particular question a student has—is an important evaluative criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt students to articulate why a method fits their interpretation of the problem (as Aleah's rotation method fit her view of the square); use fit as a discussable aesthetic dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived determinacy/precision as an aesthetic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructions that provide a clear sense of determinacy (e.g., finding intersection points with compass & perpendiculars) are perceived as more 'perfect' or precise and thus more aesthetic to some students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight how different methods convey determinacy or precision, and discuss how that affects perceived mathematical 'perfection' or reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and economy (brevity of steps, fewer constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity and economy—fewer steps, brevity of script or compactness of a method—are aesthetic criteria (e.g., Aleah's 'only six steps' versus Sara's ten).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measures like step-count, conceptual redundancy, or tool-efficiency as conversation starters about economy; note that 'simplicity' may be valued differently by different students or contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic evaluation applies beyond proofs to definitions, diagrams, methods, algorithms, theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians judge the aesthetic value of many mathematical entities including definitions, diagrams, theories, methods and algorithms—entities students encounter more frequently than finished proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden classroom aesthetic attention beyond solutions to include discussions about the elegance or suitability of definitions, representations, and procedures; ask 'Is there a better one?' about these artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide familiarity/'living through' before expecting judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Students may need to 'pick up the pencil and start working' or 'live through' a solution path before they can make meaningful aesthetic comparisons; spontaneous judgements are often premature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow time and activity to familiarise students with alternative methods; structure tasks so students can recreate or enact methods before evaluating them aesthetically (addresses why Dreyfus & Eisenberg's students reacted defensively).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic capacity as combining information and imagination for purposeful decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A student's aesthetic capacity is her ability to combine information and imagination when making purposeful decisions regarding meaning and pleasure (Dewey-inspired definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster opportunities that require both logical assessment and imaginative interpretation (e.g., variant problems, multiple representations) to develop this capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetics as a tool for engagement, memory, and meta-cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: A value-oriented sense of mathematics can engage students at a personal, humanistic level, making classroom experiences more memorable and provoking meta-cognitive reflection about feelings and beliefs regarding mathematical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aesthetic prompts to elicit reflections (why does this matter to you?), and treat student aesthetic judgements as data for encouraging meta-cognition and deeper engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers should probe student aesthetic judgements to adapt instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers can gain insight into students' thinking and feeling by probing their aesthetic judgements and can adapt teaching accordingly (e.g., leverage Aleah's perception to introduce transformational geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use students' aesthetic preferences diagnostically to inform subsequent tasks and to connect curriculum to students' ways of seeing; view aesthetics as actionable pedagogical information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting mathematics as a finished, certain body; invite evaluative questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting subject matter as finished theory—'all is calm and certain'—removes opportunities for students to ask evaluative questions like 'Is it good? Is there a better one?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design lessons that foreground mathematical negotiation, multiple viable methods, and open questions so students can practice aesthetic evaluation rather than only learning accepted results.
